user_query: How does macular edema affect visual acuity and retinal layers in preterm infants?
draft_answer:
Macular edema is common and often self-resolving in preterm infants, occurring in up to approximately 60%; its functional significance remains uncertain. Studies have reported mixed effects on visual acuity, including reduced acuity in some studies but no association in others.

Structurally, a history of macular edema is associated with thicker foveal outer retinal layers (ORL). In multivariate analysis, it was not associated with foveal inner retinal layer (IRL) thickness.

In contrast, Lee et al.28 found that a thicker ORL and thicker central macular thickness was correlated with better visual acuity in preschool age children with a history of prematurity compared to full-term born chil-dren. In BabySTEPS, we evaluated visual acuity in prema-ture infants at nine months' corrected age and found that retinal nerve fiber layer thinning across the papillomacular bundle and prior ROP treatment are associated with poorer grating visual acuity.41 Increased foveal total retinal thick-ness, but not inner retinal thickness or inner nuclear layer thickness, was associated with poorer nine-month visual acuity, but the association was only significant in univari-able analysis, although outer retinal layer thickness was not assessed.41 In addition, macular edema is a common and often self-resolving finding in preterm infants, found in up to approximately 60% of preterm infants, yet its func-tional significance is not well understood.6,9,21,23,41-43 Prior studies have reported mixed results regarding its impact, with some studies showing reduced visual acuity, poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes and others showing no asso-ciation with visual acuity.40,41,44-46 In our study, we found that infants with a history of macular edema had signifi-cantly thicker ORL compared to infants without a history of macular edema. These findings may suggest that there is likely a complex interplay between prematurity, foveal morphology, macular edema and functional outcomes, high-lighting the need for further research to elucidate these findings.

evidence.document_content: METHODS. Infants enrolled in the STudy of Eye imaging in Preterm infantS (BabySTEPS1; NCT02887157) were imaged at four and nine months' corrected age. For infants with grad-able imaging, foveal and parafoveal inner (IRL) and outer (ORL) retinal layer thicknesses were measured, with parafoveal/foveal thickness (P/F) ratios calculated. Univariate and multivariate regression analyses were performed to determine associations of birth and perinatal factors with foveation, and the effect of gestational age (GA) and history of macular edema on foveal thickness measurements. Citation: Zhou XY, Ying GS, Tai V, Mangalesh S, Toth CA, Chen X. Effect of prematurity on foveal development during infancy: Increased foveal inner and outer retina layer thicknesses in extremely premature infants. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci. 2026;67(12):4. https://doi.org/10.1167/iovs.67.12.4 RESULTS. In multivariate analysis of 99 eyes (56 infants) at four months and 70 eyes (44 infants, 34 infants overlapped with the four-months group) at nine months' corrected age, decreased P/F ratio was associated with lower GA (per week decrease) (four months: β (SE) = -0.109 (0.010, P < 0.0001; nine months: β (SE) = -0.063(0.011), P = 0.0005). Lower GA was associated with thicker foveal IRL (four months: β (SE) = 5.91 (0.76) μm, P < 0.0001; nine months: β (SE) = 3.95 (0.99) μm, P = 0.004) and ORL (four months: β (SE) = 4.86 (1.10) μm, P = 0.003; nine months: β (SE) = 4.46 (1.13) μm, P = 0.002). History of macular edema was associated with higher P/F ratios and thicker foveal ORL but not foveal IRL.

In univariate analysis (Table 5), foveal IRL was signifi-cantly thicker in infants with a history of macular edema at nine months, but not at four months. This trend persisted when INL was factored into the IRL measurement (Tables 5, 6). However, in multivariate analysis (Table 6), foveal IRL was not associated with history of macular edema. Prior studies have established that individuals with a history of prematurity demonstrate altered foveal development char-acterized by increased central foveal thickness, retained IRLs, and increased ORL thickness at school age and in adulthood.6,23,25-30 We previously evaluated foveation in a large cohort of infants before term age and found arrested foveation in the extremely premature infants throughout the preterm period.8 However, how these changes evolved after term age in the first year of life remained unknown. In the present study, we addressed this gap in knowledge of foveation in preterm infants during infancy by evaluating foveal development in the same cohort of infants during their first year of life. chunks.document_content: Macular edema is frequently observed in premature infants before term-equivalent age.21-23 A trained grader manually evaluated for the presence of macular edema based on the presence of cystoid changes, typically in the inner nuclear layer (INL), and determined severity of edema based on deformation of the inner retinal contour at the foveal center. O'Sullivan et al. used a cut-off INL thickness of 71.25 μm (averaged over central 2000 μm) as an objective measure of macular edema.8 In this manuscript, we also used this value as a threshold to evaluate the presence of macular edema. Because macular edema in premature infants is tran-sient, an eye was classified as having a history of macular edema if edema was identified at any prior gradable imag-ing visit based on grader assessment and/or INL thickness of ≥71.25 μm). This study was conducted in preterm infants undergoing ROP screening as a part of the prospective, observational STudy of Eye imaging in Preterm infantS (BabySTEPS1; Clin-icalTrials.gov, NCT02887157). The study was approved by Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board and adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and the guidelines of Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Informed consent was obtained from the parent/legal guardian for study participation after expla-nation of the nature and possible consequences of the study. Imaging analysis and grading were performed as previously described.8 Briefly, for each imaging session, a single hori-zontal B-scan that best captured the fovea from the best foveal volume was manually selected by a senior OCT image grader masked to clinical history except age at time of imag-ing. The foveal center was identified based on the presence of an inner retinal divot or the point of minimal inner retinal thickness. Retinal layer segmentation was performed using a semi-automated, infant-specific segmentation algorithm with manual correction as needed using proprietary infant-specific software he Duke OCT Retinal Analysis Program Marking Code Baby version 1.2 or 2.0 (MATLAB; MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA). Total retinal thickness was measured from the internal limiting membrane to the inner border of the retinal pigment epithelium. Inner retinal layer (IRL) was measured from the internal limiting membrane to the inner border of INL. ORL was measured from the outer border of INL to the inner border of retinal pigment epithelium. The INL was excluded from the IRL measurement to avoid poten-tial effects of macular edema. Like Anwar et al.,18 although later in life of preterm infants, we found that the foveal ORL remains thickest in the most premature infants. In school age and older preterm born patients, the transient phenomenon of INL edema in the preterm period had not been recorded. This study demonstrates the persisting impact of that event on outer retinal morphology in the first year of life. Several studies comparing preterm to full-term children or adults have also found that the foveal ORL was thicker in indi-viduals with history of prematurity.8,29,32-34 One possible mechanism for this thickening was suggested by Sjostrand et al.,29 who proposed that the arrested outward migration of IRL results in a weakened outward pull on the synaptically connected cone pedicles and photoreceptor cell bodies. As a consequence, their axons adopt a more vertical orientation centrally, increasing the thickness of the ORL.
